blocks.prompt: A Crab Wears Its Bones Outside
blocks.text: Your bones are inside you. A crab keeps its bones on the outside. Its hard shell is like a little suit of armor, and the soft crab lives inside it. A crab has ten legs. The two front legs are claws. It grabs food with its claws. It walks on the other eight legs. A crab walks sideways because its legs bend that way. A crab breathes with gills, like a fish does. Its gills have to stay wet, so the crab stays near the water. A crab's eyes sit on two little stalks. It can lift them up to look around. It can fold them down to keep them safe.

blocks.prompt: Why a Crab Walks Sideways
blocks.text: Watch a crab cross a beach and you will notice something odd. It does not run forward. It scuttles sideways, one side leading and the other side following. The reason is in its knees. Your leg bends forward and back, so forward is the easy way for you to go. A crab's legs bend the other way. Each joint hinges out to the side. Pushing off sideways lets a crab swing all eight walking legs at once without tripping over itself. Sideways is not clumsy for a crab. Sideways is its fastest gear. The rest of the crab is built for the same job. Its body is wide and flat, so it can slide into a crack between two rocks and sit there while a hungry bird gives up and leaves. Its eyes ride on two stalks that swivel, so it can watch behind itself while it runs. Its claws stay out in front like a pair of shields. Not every crab goes sideways. Some spider crabs amble slowly forward, and some crabs have flat back legs and swim. But for a crab out on open sand, with a gull circling above, sideways is the move that works.

blocks.prompt: The Crab That Climbs Out of Itself
blocks.text: A crab has a problem you do not have. Your skeleton is inside you, and it grows as you grow. A crab's skeleton is on the outside, a hard case of armor, and armor does not stretch. So a crab that wants to get bigger has to get out of its own body first. The process is called molting. Before it begins, the crab grows a soft new shell underneath the old one, folded and wrinkled like a shirt packed into a suitcase. Then it takes on water until it swells. The old shell splits open along the back edge, and the crab begins to reverse out through the gap. Every part has to come free: eight legs, two claws, both eyestalks, even the lining of its gills and the inside of its stomach. It can take hours, and a crab that gets stuck does not get a second try. What backs out is a soft, pale, floppy crab. For a few days it is nearly defenseless, so it hides under a rock and keeps pumping in water, holding the new shell stretched wide while it hardens. That extra water is the room the crab will grow into later. Some crabs eat the old shell to take back the calcium in it. Molting comes with a bonus. If a crab loses a leg, a small replacement bud forms, and with each molt the bud grows bigger, until one day the leg is whole again. A crab caught by a gull can even snap off its own claw at a special weak joint and scuttle away, leaving the bird holding a souvenir. Losing a claw is bad. Losing all of yourself is worse.

blocks.prompt: The Island That Closes Its Roads for Crabs
blocks.text: Christmas Island is a small piece of Australia in the Indian Ocean, and for most of the year it looks like ordinary rainforest. Then the first heavy rain of the wet season falls, and the forest floor starts to move. Tens of millions of red crabs live on Christmas Island. They spend their lives inland, in burrows under the leaf litter, eating fallen leaves and keeping the forest floor clear. But a red crab cannot start a family on land. Its eggs have to hatch in salt water, the way its ancestors' eggs did. So once a year, when the rain arrives and the moon is right, nearly every adult crab on the island walks to the ocean. They do not go around obstacles. They go over them. The migration crosses roads, gardens, cliffs, and parking lots in a red flood that takes days to pass. The island responds by getting out of the way. Rangers close roads for weeks. Plastic barriers steer the crabs into concrete underpasses. In one place a steel bridge arcs above a road, built for nothing but crabs. The timing is not luck. The females release their eggs at dawn, at the turn of a high tide, in the last quarter of the moon, when the gap between high water and low water is smallest and the surf is least likely to smash them against the rocks. The eggs burst the instant they touch the sea. The larvae drift offshore for about a month, and the survivors return as crabs the size of a fingernail, then walk inland to a forest they have never seen. There is a shadow over all of this. Yellow crazy ants arrived on the island by accident, hidden in cargo. They spray acid that blinds and kills red crabs, and in a few decades they destroyed an estimated ten to fifteen million of them. Scientists are fighting back with a tiny introduced wasp that attacks the insects the ants feed on. It is a strange kind of war, fought with wasps over crabs, and the crabs themselves have no idea it is happening. They just keep walking to the sea.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: True crabs belong to Brachyura, meaning short tail

Count the legs: a true crab shows four walking pairs

blocks.prompt: Nature Keeps Making Crabs
blocks.text: Here is a fact that sounds like a joke and is not. Evolution cannot seem to stop making crabs. Start with what a crab actually is. To a biologist, a true crab belongs to a group called Brachyura, a word that means short tail. The name is the whole clue. A lobster carries its long muscular abdomen out behind it, and that is the part people eat as a tail. A true crab has the same abdomen, but folded flat and tucked underneath its body like a hand in a pocket. Widen the shell, flatten it, tuck the tail away, and you have the shape everyone recognizes. Now the strange part. That shape has appeared over and over, in lineages that are not closely related to true crabs at all. King crabs, the big spiny ones sold as legs in restaurants, are not descended from true crabs. Their ancestors were hermit crabs, soft animals that spent their lives hiding inside borrowed snail shells. The king crab body was built from scratch, on a separate branch of the family tree. Porcelain crabs, coconut crabs, hairy stone crabs: crab shaped, every one of them, and each arrived at that shape by its own road. Biologists count at least five independent origins of the crab form among the ten-legged crustaceans. In 1916 a zoologist named Borradaile noticed the pattern and named it carcinization, describing it as nature's repeated attempt to make a crab. You can catch the impostors by counting. A true crab shows four pairs of walking legs plus a pair of claws. The false crabs have shrunk their last pair of legs and folded them up under the shell, where the legs are used to clean the gills, so the animal appears to be walking on six. Female king crabs also carry a lopsided abdomen, a leftover from ancestors who spent their lives curled inside a spiral shell. Why would the same body keep reappearing? Nobody is certain, but the leading answer is that the crab shape solves several problems at once. A wide flat body slides into rock cracks that a long-tailed animal cannot enter. A tucked abdomen hides the softest, most bitable part of the animal. Sideways walking, which those outward-hinged joints make efficient, suits an uneven seafloor. When unrelated animals face the same pressures in the same places, natural selection tends to hand them the same answer. That is convergent evolution, the same reason wings turned up separately in birds, bats, and insects. The pattern also runs backward. Some crab lineages have partly undone it, untucking the abdomen and stretching out again once their lives changed. So evolution is not marching toward crabs. It is not marching anywhere at all. It is simply that in a world of hard rocks, tight spaces, and hungry mouths, the crab is an answer the ocean keeps rediscovering.
